rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thamūd exemplifies a people who obscure the soul through disobedience; the northern Arabian tribe rejected the Prophet Ṣāliḥ.
rows.anchor: The tribe of Thamūd is cited as an example of those who “obscure” the soul through disobedience.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣāliḥ identified the she-camel brought from a rock as God's sign and called the people to justice and God's ordained sharing of water.
rows.anchor: Ṣāliḥ made it clear to them that a particular she-camel that God had brought forth from a rock was a sign of God

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: They had agreed the she-camel drank one day and other animals the next, and killed her because they disliked the arrangement.
rows.anchor: According to some commentators, they had agreed that the she-camel would drink one day and the other animals would drink the next

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet identified those who hamstrung the she-camel as the most wretched people of earlier generations.
rows.anchor: It is recorded that the Prophet said that the most wretched of previous generations

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some interpret ʿaqqarūhā as saying that they slaughtered the she-camel.
rows.anchor: Some interpret hamstrung her (ʿaqqarūhā) as “slaughtered her”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Damdama describes an exceptionally severe punishment that came suddenly and annihilated and entirely covered the people.
rows.anchor: indicates the most severe of punishments

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sawwāhā can mean God razed their city or leveled the earth over them, or distributed the same punishment to every tribe member.
rows.anchor: It could also be rendered, “He distributed it equally,” meaning that God distributed the same punishment upon every member of the tribe

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Using sawwā for both human creation and destruction suggests God destroys as easily as He creates and that punishment continues His fashioning of the soul.
rows.anchor: The use of sawwā in this context, in relation to both the creation of human beings in v. 7 and their destruction in v. 14

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr; al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: God fears no consequence from destroying a people like Thamūd; this warns Quraysh that God needs nothing from them and can likewise wipe them out.
rows.anchor: This verse means that God does not fear the consequences of destroying a people like the tribe of Thamūd

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Alternatively, the subject is the most wretched man, who heedlessly hamstrung the camel without fearing the outcome of his act.
rows.anchor: the subject is either the most wretched (v. 12), who hamstrung the she-camel and did not fear the outcome of his actions

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Alternatively, Ṣāliḥ did not fear the outcome because he had delivered God's message and was spared the people's punishment.
rows.anchor: or the Prophet Ṣāliḥ, who did not fear the outcome because he had fulfilled his duty by transmitting God’s message

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: An alternate reading is “By the creation of the male and female”; some consider it more fitting because God would not swear by Himself.
rows.anchor: Another reading is, “By the creation of the male and female” (Q, Sh). As with 91:5–7, some maintain this second reading is more appropriate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Male and female can symbolize the outward polarity of forms, paired with the surah's inward polarity between reverers of truth and its deniers.
rows.anchor: The reference to the male and female can be seen as an allusion to the outward polarity of created forms

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse also implies gender does not determine the final end; reverence does, as affirmed in the address to humanity in 49:13.
rows.anchor: the final ends of both males and females are not determined by their gender, but by the degree of their reverence

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr; al-Qurṭubī; al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Some understand God's guidance here as explaining what is lawful and prohibited.
rows.anchor: Some understand this verse to mean, “We will explain what is lawful and what is prohibited”

rows.speaker: Ibn Kathīr
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that whoever follows guidance will reach God in the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Others take it to indicate that one who travels the path of guidance will reach God in the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse parallels the teaching that God alone has the role of showing the way.
rows.anchor: It can also be likened to other verses that explain that it is God’s place to guide and no one else’s

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some read God's ownership of both abodes as referring to their reward, and by implication their worldly and otherworldly punishment as well.
rows.anchor: Some commentators see this verse as a reference to the reward of the Hereafter and this world

rows.speaker: Sh
rows.claim: Others understand the verse to say everything belongs to God and He disposes of it as He wills.
rows.anchor: Others see this verse as an indication that everything is God’s and He does with it as He wills

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hell is elsewhere described as a crushing Fire.
rows.anchor: Elsewhere Hell is described as a crushing Fire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording literally says the last is better than the first; Quranic teaching generally makes the Hereafter better than worldly life, which is fleeting enjoyment.
rows.anchor: This verse literally reads, “And the last shall be better for thee than the first.” Throughout the Quran the Abode of the Hereafter is considered better

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran condemns those who trade away the Hereafter for worldly life.
rows.anchor: The Quran thus criticizes those who have purchased the world at the price of the Hereafter

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet chose to be with God in the Hereafter rather than remain in this life until its end and then enter Paradise.
rows.anchor: It is reported that when the Prophet was given the choice between remaining in this life until the end of time

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās relates that the Prophet asked for a favor, then God recalled blessings including shelter as an orphan, guidance, enrichment, an expanded breast, and a lifted burden.
rows.anchor: Ibn ʿAbbās reported that the Prophet said, “I have asked my Lord for something I wish I had not asked for.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After his father died before his birth and his mother when he was six, the Prophet was successively cared for by his grandfather and uncle Abū Ṭālib, who protected him; Khadījah was also a refuge.
rows.anchor: After this he was under the guardianship of his grandfather,ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib, until he died when the Prophet was eight years old.

rows.speaker: al-Baghawī
rows.claim: One reading is that God taught Muhammad his true nature as God's messenger.
rows.anchor: This verse can be taken as reference to God’s teaching Muhammad his true nature as a messenger of God

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: A literal reading says Muhammad was astray until God guided him to monotheism and prophethood.
rows.anchor: Some understand this verse literally to mean that Muhammad had been astray and that God guided him to belief in the Oneness of God

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others say the Prophet lacked a revealed law or rite, unknown to his people, without having strayed from monotheistic belief.
rows.anchor: For others, this verse means that the Prophet had strayed in the sense that he did not follow a revealed law or rite

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A related reading is that Muhammad believed in God's Oneness but had neither scripture nor direct guidance before the Quran was revealed.
rows.anchor: although he believed in the Oneness of God, he had no scripture and no direct guidance until the Quran was revealed

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: To avoid religious implications, some take the verse to refer to Muhammad being lost in Makkah's streets until Gabriel guided him.
rows.anchor: Some try to avoid the implication that the Prophet could have been astray in any religious or spiritual sense

rows.speaker: still others
rows.claim: Another report says the Prophet's mount strayed from the road during a journey and Gabriel returned him to the way.
rows.anchor: Still others see it as a reference to a time when the Prophet was on a journey, his mount strayed from the road

rows.speaker: al-Baghawī
rows.claim: One view takes God's enrichment of the Prophet as material wealth through his first wife Khadījah.
rows.anchor: Some understand this verse as a reference to the Prophet’s enrichment through the wealth of his first wife, Khadījah

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others understand the true wealth to be spiritual contentment, as in the hadith that wealth is wealth of the soul rather than abundance of goods.
rows.anchor: Others say it refers to the true wealth, which is spiritual contentment

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command reminds the Prophet of his own orphanhood and, more broadly, admonishes Quraysh for taking orphans' wealth and violating their rights.
rows.anchor: On one level, this verse serves as a reminder from God that the Prophet should remember his own state as an orphan.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other revelations command justice for orphans and forbid approaching their property except in the best manner.
rows.anchor: Muslims are enjoined, Approach not the orphan’s property, save in the best manner

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith calls the best Muslim home one that treats an orphan well and the worst one that mistreats an orphan; the Prophet likens an orphan's caretaker and himself to two adjacent fingers in the Garden.
rows.anchor: The best house among the Muslims is a house in which an orphan has been treated well.

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: The verse enjoins kindness toward beggars, especially by feeding the one who comes to the door or gently turning the person away.
rows.anchor: this verse is seen by most commentators as a specific reference to the beggar who comes to the door

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request may also be a request for religious knowledge, making the verse an instruction to share it with seekers.
rows.anchor: It is also interpreted as an exhortation to share knowledge of the religion with anyone who seeks it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is commanded to spread God's blessings through thanks and praise.
rows.anchor: This verse is a command to the Prophet meaning, “Spread that with which God has blessed thee through thanks and praise”

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The blessing may mean the Quran, prophethood, guidance after the mention of being astray, or any blessing God bestows.
rows.anchor: The blessing of thy Lord can refer to the Quran itself

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A sermon hadith says gratitude for little and for people is necessary, proclaiming God's blessings is gratitude, and abandoning it is disbelief.
rows.anchor: proclaiming [God’s] blessings is thanks, while abandoning it [i.e., proclaiming God’s Blessings] is disbelief

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A report says the Prophet rejoiced at the surah's revelation, proclaimed God's greatness, and advised followers to do likewise when reciting it.
rows.anchor: when this sūrah was revealed, the Prophet was joyous, proclaimed, “God is great

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Expansion of the breast signifies ease, especially in religious matters, and characterizes the rightly guided; Moses' prayer asks for this ease.
rows.anchor: The expansion of the breast relates to ease, especially in matters pertaining to religion

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Constricted breasts characterize the astray, though even the rightly guided can feel constriction in trials; here it may allude to patience granted to bear enemies' insults.
rows.anchor: Those who are rightly guided can also experience straitening of the breast through trials and hardship.

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The expansion can mean God made the Prophet's heart a receptacle for revelation's wisdom, prophethood, and knowledge.
rows.anchor: this verse has also been seen as an allusion to the manner in which God expanded the Prophet’s breast and made his heart a container for the wisdom

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some connect the verse to relief after the Prophet's solitude on Mount Ḥirāʾ.
rows.anchor: According to some, this verse refers to the relief that came to the Prophet’s breast after a period of solitude on Mt. Ḥirāʾ.

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others connect it to the end of the reported interruption in revelation.
rows.anchor: According to others, it refers to the end of a period in which the revelation was said to have been interrupted

rows.speaker: still others
rows.claim: Still others read it as the Prophet's childhood chest-opening episode, when two angels removed a dark clot representing the soul's root of malice and envy.
rows.anchor: Still others read it as a reference to an episode in the Prophet’s youth when two angels opened his breast

rows.speaker: many commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators take lifting the burden as an allusion to the Prophet being forgiven all his sins.
rows.anchor: This verse is seen by many commentators as an allusion to the Prophet’s being forgiven all sins

rows.speaker: al-Bayḍāwī
rows.claim: Anqaḍa describes a load pressing so heavily that the back makes a sound.
rows.anchor: one’s back makes a sound (Bḍ).

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some read the burden as the weight of prophethood.
rows.anchor: Some say this verse refers to God’s lightening the burden of prophethood

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Verses 2–3 may describe removing Arabia's ignorance and confusion through revelation's laws and decrees.
rows.anchor: Vv. 2–3 can also be seen as a reference to the lifting of the burden of ignorance and confusion

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: The Prophet's renown rose through the title Messenger of God and its inclusion with God's Name in the testimony of faith, call to prayer, and prayer's closing greeting.
rows.anchor: a title connected with the Name of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The strongest sign of Muhammad's renown is God's and the angels' blessing on him, which believers are commanded to invoke.
rows.anchor: The strongest indicator of the Prophet’s great renown is in 33:56

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some identify the elevated renown with blessings upon the Prophet; others with his mention in earlier scriptures.
rows.anchor: According to some it is such blessings to which v. 4 refers

rows.speaker: al-Bayḍāwī; al-Jalālayn; al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: One reading is: after obligatory devotions, turn to supplication and supererogatory worship.
rows.anchor: after completing the obligatory devotions, one should supplicate the Lord and perform supererogatory devotions

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Another reading says that when free from worldly affairs one should pray.
rows.anchor: when free from worldly affairs, one should pray

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further reading urges one, once devoted to God, continually to deepen prayer.
rows.anchor: So when thou art devoted [to God], exert thyself,” meaning that one should always seek to deepen one’s prayers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the phrase means when spent, it calls for unceasing striving in God's way and in doing His will.
rows.anchor: So when thou art spent, toil,” meaning one should never cease to strive in the way of God

rows.speaker: al-Bayḍāwī; al-Shāfiʿī; al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: Another interpretation is to worship the Lord after being free from striving against enemies.
rows.anchor: When thou art free from striving against thine enemies, exert thyself in worshipping the Lord

rows.speaker: al-Ṭabarī
rows.claim: The command means not to desire this world and to direct desire to God alone.
rows.anchor: This verse is understood to mean, “Do not desire this world—let your desire be for God alone”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse exhorts prayer and insists that prayer and good deeds be directed only to please God.
rows.anchor: On the one hand, this is an exhortation to prayer; on the other, it is an exhortation to pray only to God

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most identify the named Mount Sinai with the Mount in eight other verses, though some dispute those identifications.
rows.anchor: According to most commentators, Mount Sinai is also referred to by name in 23:20 and simply as the Mount

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some derive sinīn from Ethiopic for beautiful and read the phrase as the blessed beautiful Mount; others take it to mean any mountain bearing fruit trees.
rows.anchor: some say is actually taken from the Ethiopic for “beautiful” and in this context means “the blessed beautiful Mount”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pre-Islamic Makkah was a secure refuge where fighting was forbidden.
rows.anchor: In pre-Islamic Arabia Makkah was a refuge in which no fighting was allowed

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some interpret the fig and olive as Jerusalem and Jesus, Sinai as where God spoke to Moses, and the secure land as where Muhammad was sent.
rows.anchor: Some say that the fig and the olive (v. 1) is a reference to Jerusalem, where Jesus was sent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question addresses people who deny revelation, resurrection, and other parts of religion.
rows.anchor: As translated, this verse is a question posed to those who deny the revelation, the Resurrection, and other aspects of religion.

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Another reading addresses belief in the Prophet: after the proofs, who could deny the Messenger; some consider this grammatically problematic.
rows.anchor: It may also be addressing belief in the Prophet specifically

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse expresses amazement that people who came from a drop and attained beautiful stature still deny resurrection.
rows.anchor: The verse also indicates amazement that anyone could witness human beings coming from a drop

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since some descend from the most beautiful stature to the lowest and others remain elevated, God's just judgment logically assigns them different recompenses.
rows.anchor: the implication is that human beings differ, because some leave the state of the most beautiful stature and descend to the lowest of the low

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Al-ʿAlaq is an early Makkan surah; most regard its first five verses as the Quran's first revelation, with the rest revealed later amid Quraysh opposition.
rows.anchor: The first five verses are considered by most to be the first verses of the Quran to be revealed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first revelation is dated to Ramadan's last third in 610 CE, twelve years before the 622 Hijrah that began the Islamic calendar.
rows.anchor: This initial revelation is said to have taken place during the last third of the month of Ramadan, in 610 of the Christian era

rows.speaker: ʿĀʾishah
rows.claim: ʿĀʾishah recounts the Prophet's true dreams, growing love of solitude and worship in Ḥirāʾ, Gabriel's three commands to recite and pressing him, and his fear on returning to Khadījah; she comforted him, then brought him to Waraqah, who recognized Mosaic revelation and predicted his people's hostility and expulsion, promising support.
rows.anchor: According to the Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾishah, “The first thing that began happening with the Messenger of God from the revelation were dreams he would see in his sleep

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah opens with recitation, admonishes humanity and then those preventing religious practice, and ends by challenging reliance on protectors besides God.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with an injunction to recite (vv. 1–5) followed by an admonition of mankind in general

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first mention of creation may mean that God creates all existence from nothing.
rows.anchor: The first mention of creation in v. 1 can be taken as a reference to the fact that God creates all that exists from nothing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human being is honored through knowledge, which distinguishes Adam from the angels; humanity is created to know God and creation, and God taught Adam the names before commanding, legislating, and judging.
rows.anchor: The passage then moves to the creation of the human being, who is honored and ennobled through knowledge

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Recitation precedes writing because speech can exist without writing, whereas writing cannot exist without speech; “recite” is better than “read” because the Prophet had no text to read and was unlettered.
rows.anchor: there could be speech without writing, but not writing without speech

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blood clot appears as gestation's third stage in the Quran's fullest account, followed by a lump of flesh and further stages.
rows.anchor: The blood clot appears to be the third stage in the most extensive Quranic account of gestation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–2 may explain 95:4–5: creation refers to man's beautiful stature and the clot to his casting down to the lowest.
rows.anchor: Vv. 1–2 can also be seen as a commentary on 95:4–5

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pre-Islamic karāmah meant nobility and magnanimity, including noble lineage, virtuous character, and generosity.
rows.anchor: was considered the highest of all virtues

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Most generous” is another sense: God gives creation and revelation, while Quranic use of karīm for God introduced the pagan Arabs to a new divine attribute.
rows.anchor: this verse could also be understood to mean, “Recite, for thy Lord is most generous,”

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Three principal pens are described: the divine Logos or Intellect recording all until the Resurrection, angelic pens recording human deeds, and human writing pens.
rows.anchor: Some say that pens are of three principal types: the first, corresponding to the Logos or Intellect

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some take “man” as Adam, taught all the names; others as Muhammad, taught the Book and Wisdom; most commentators take it to mean all humanity.
rows.anchor: But here most commentators take taught man to mean that this verse refers to the manner in which God teaches all human beings

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Teaching by the Pen is also an allusion to Divine Intellect inscribing knowledge on the human soul, continuing God's generosity and bringing people from darkness into light.
rows.anchor: God’s teaching by the Pen can also be seen as an allusion to the Divine Intellect inscribing knowledge upon the tablet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The later verses reportedly came years after the first five, concerning Abū Jahl, Quraysh's leader, who rejected Muhammad's prophethood and obstructed Islam.
rows.anchor: These verses were reportedly revealed several years after vv. 1–5 in reference to Abū Jahl, the leader of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic kallā rebukes people for denying and failing to thank God for creation and knowledge; rebellion includes resistance to God's teaching.
rows.anchor: kallā) here implies that despite the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Self-sufficiency conveys a negative claim to independence from God and is the root of rebelliousness.
rows.anchor: Beyond need is literally “self-sufficient,” but beyond need better conveys the negative connotation

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Return to God is among the Quran's central themes.
rows.anchor: The return to God is among the most central themes of the Quran

rows.speaker: usually understood
rows.claim: The prohibition of a worshipping servant is usually taken as Abū Jahl preventing the Prophet from praying at the Kaʿbah.
rows.anchor: a direct reference to AbūJahl’s preventing the Prophet from praying

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The questions rebuke Abū Jahl by asking whether he can judge the Prophet's guidance, while applying generally to those who challenge the Prophet and Quran.
rows.anchor: These verses are taken as a rebuke to Abū Jahl

rows.speaker: some; others
rows.claim: Some read the pronoun through verses 11–12 as referring to the Prophet; others take it to refer to Abū Jahl.
rows.anchor: Although some take vv.13–14 as a continuation of the admonishment in vv. 11–12

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most take the threat as answering verse 14: Abū Jahl fails to recognize God's sight and would persist in blocking the Prophet; the warning also applies generally.
rows.anchor: These verses are taken by most as an answer to v. 14, meaning that Abū Jahl did not know that God sees.

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Cohorts means other Quraysh supporters of Abū Jahl.
rows.anchor: Cohorts is seen by most as a reference to the other members of the Quraysh who supported Abū Jahl.

rows.speaker: Ibn ʿAbbās
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās reports that Abū Jahl threatened the praying Prophet with his many guards, prompting these verses; Ibn ʿAbbās says God would have sent Hell's guards had Abū Jahl called his men.
rows.anchor: According to Ibn ʿAbbās, the Prophet was praying when Abū Jahl came to him and said

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Nay” can rebuke Abū Jahl or address the Prophet and followers to ignore his threats and continue prostrating.
rows.anchor: Nay is either another rebuke to Abū Jahl or an address directly to the Prophet and his followers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: More generally, believers should ignore denials of religion or prayer and draw near to God through prostration; a hadith says prostration is a servant's closest state to the Lord.
rows.anchor: The closest that a servant can be to his Lord is when he is prostrating

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is one of fifteen verses after whose recitation prostration is enjoined.
rows.anchor: This verse is one of fifteen verses after the recitation of which one is enjoined to prostrate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qadr is early Makkan and believed revealed after 80: ʿAbasa; it concerns the Night of Power, when the Quran was first revealed, in Ramadan.
rows.anchor: al-Qadr is believed to have been revealed after Sūrah 80, ʿAbasa.

rows.speaker: many reports
rows.claim: Muslims hold the Night of Power returns annually; many place it in Ramadan's last ten nights and most, based on a hadith, on an odd-numbered one.
rows.anchor: Many reports say that the Night of Power occurs during the last ten nights of Ramadan

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet practiced retreat during Ramadan's last ten days, abstained from conjugal relations, fasted and prayed at night, and advised followers to do likewise.
rows.anchor: The Prophet himself would usually practice spiritual retreat

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith promises forgiveness of previous sins to one who prays on the Night of Power with faith and hope for reward.
rows.anchor: Whoever stands [in prayer] during the Night of Power out of belief and seeking reward, his previous sins are forgiven

rows.speaker: Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet advised asking God, a pardoner who loves pardon, for forgiveness that night.
rows.anchor: My God, truly thou art a pardoner who loves pardoning; so pardon me

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This surah pairs with the next: it treats transmission of revelation, while the next stresses acting in accordance with it.
rows.anchor: This sūrah can be understood as forming a pair with the following sūrah

rows.speaker: several commentators
rows.claim: “It” is the Quran, and several commentators say it was revealed all at once in a first stage from the Preserved Tablet to the lowest heaven or specifically the House of Might; gradual revelation followed over 23 years, 610–632.
rows.anchor: According to several commentators, these verses indicate that the Quran was revealed in its entirety at once

rows.speaker: Mujāhid
rows.claim: Mujāhid calls the Night of Power the night of judgment or decree, when God decrees the coming year, or the decree for all creation.
rows.anchor: According to Mujāhid, it is “the night of ḥukm,” “the night of judgment/decree”

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Some say the night's name signifies its honor and greatness, with no necessary connection to decree.
rows.anchor: Others do not see a necessary relation to God’s Decree, saying that this night is so named to convey its honor and greatness

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others link its name to the great power and reward of obedience and worship performed that night.
rows.anchor: Others say that the name relates to the power of acts of obedience and worship performed during it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical question emphatically conveys the night's holiness and that true knowledge of it lies beyond human understanding with God.
rows.anchor: The rhetorical question in v. 2 is an emphatic expression of the utter holiness of this night

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship that night merits more than worship in a thousand other months; a thousand may emphasize greatness rather than denote an exact count, or mean all time.
rows.anchor: The merit for acts of worship performed during this night is greater than that for those performed during a thousand other months

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels descend to bless believers and bring peace, a function affirmed in hadiths as occurring beyond this night but especially effulgent on it.
rows.anchor: On this night the angels descend to bless and bring peace to the believers

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most identify the Spirit as Gabriel, the angel of revelation.
rows.anchor: Most interpret the Spirit as a reference to the Archangel Gabriel, who is the angel of revelation

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Alternative readings identify the Spirit as the noblest angels, angels at the Lote Tree, a special descending angel group, another archangel, or God's Mercy.
rows.anchor: others say it is a reference to a type of angel, those who are the most noble of them

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Fīhā can mean “among them,” so the Spirit descends together with the angels.
rows.anchor: could also be taken to mean “among them,” meaning that the Spirit descends with the angels

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: “By the leave of their Lord” may mean by their Lord's command, as the angels say in 19:64.
rows.anchor: By the leave of their Lord is interpreted by some to mean “by the Command of their Lord”

rows.speaker: most prevalent interpretation
rows.claim: “Every command” may mean every decree God has ordained for the following year.
rows.anchor: The most prevalent is that it means on account of everything that God has ordained (qaḍā) for the following year

rows.speaker: alternate reading
rows.claim: An alternate reading, min kulli imriʾin, means “for every human being.”
rows.anchor: An alternate reading of this verse is min kulli imriʾin, meaning, “for every human being”

rows.speaker: many
rows.claim: Many say the angels greet with peace those who spend the night in prayer.
rows.anchor: Many say this verse refers to greetings of peace that the angels bestow upon those who spend this night in prayer

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others take the night itself to be entirely peaceful, without evil.
rows.anchor: Others say it indicates that this night itself is naught but peace

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some say peace characterizes everything God decrees for the coming year during this night.
rows.anchor: Some say it indicates that there is peace in everything that God decrees or ordains for the following year

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse may evoke pregnant quietude before the Divine Word's emergence in the human world and the heart's stillness for true remembrance.
rows.anchor: It can also be seen as conveying the pregnant quietude that precedes the emergence of the Divine Word in the human world

rows.speaker: many commentators; others
rows.claim: Many classify al-Bayyinah as Madinan, while others regard it as Makkan; it is named for the clear proof and also called lam yakun and al-Qiyāmah.
rows.anchor: any commentators take al-Bayyinah to be a Madinan sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayyinah derives from bayyana, meaning to make or become clear; Quranic clarity marks revelation and prophetic teaching and distinguishes truth from concealment and caprice.
rows.anchor: Bayyinah derives from the verb bayyana, meaning “to make or to become clear, evident, manifest, plain, or apparent,”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All revelation is presented as clear proof; Moses, Jesus, and other prophets also came with proofs, contrasting truth-followers with those who reject them.
rows.anchor: and other prophets as having come with clear

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening says disbelievers oppose the Prophet until clear proof comes; the last three verses contrast disbelievers' and believers' fates.
rows.anchor: The sūrah begins with an assertion that those who disbelieve will continue to oppose the Prophet until a clear proof comes to them
